anchorLine: τος πρὸς τὸ μετεχόμενόν ἐστι θέωσις τῶν ἀξιουμένων θεώσεως *.
en: Many more things follow in that question 59 (of the Questions to Thalassius), worthy of Maximus's own vein.

text: Ἡ ἄρρητος περιχώρησις τοῦ πεπιστευμένου. Alia profano usu hujus vocis significatio, quam hic conveniat. Quod vero reddit Picus, arcana processio, non satisfacit; nec satis video quid ea voce velit. Budæus longe doctior in Damasceno de Trinit. divinam personarum περιχώρησιν, unionem reddit; quod forte paulo liberius est: theologi circumincessionem vocant, quasi unius personæ in aliam undique immeationem; malim ego, quod una capiat aliam ac velut contineat et comprehendat; quomodo etiam dicuntur divinæ personæ ἀνεκφοιτήτως procedere, ita ut alia extra aliam non excedant: quæ vocis χωρεῖν, trita admodum significatio est, soletque et ad animum transferri, quod ille quasi continendo ac in se rem habendo, intelligat. Sic ergo Maximum intelligo. Manifestationem ac revelationem rei creditæ ac Dei (quæ fit per dona Spiritus adjuvantia fidem) ejus in nobis comprehensionem esse ac perceptionem: ut hinc in nobis habitantem habeamus ipsumque præsentem ac nobis intimum cognoscamus, juxta illud Pauli (Ephes. iii, 17): Habitare Christum per fidem in cordibus vestris. Nec istud vetat aliquid arcanam unionem dicere, et quasi commistionem, juxta quod Hesych. περιχωρεῖ, συμμίσγεται exponit. Sed in his balbutimus, etsi Græci paulo nobis vocibus sunt feliciores. In aliis, nihil fere Picus felicior, ut quod ἀεικίνητος στάσις, illi est, conditio semper movens; non quia jugi incitata motu; qualis fruentium Deo.
en: 'The ineffable perichoresis of what is believed.' The word has another sense in profane usage than the one suited here. Picus's 'arcane procession' does not satisfy, and the editor does not see what he means by it. Budaeus, a far more learned man, rendered the divine perichoresis of the persons in Damascene's De Trinitate as 'union', which is perhaps a little loose; theologians call it circumincession, as if one person's penetration all around into another; the editor would prefer: that one takes in the other and as it were contains and comprehends it, as the divine persons are also said to proceed without going out of one another (anekphoitos), so that none passes beyond another. The verb chorein has a worn-out sense and is often transferred to the mind, because it understands by containing and having the thing in itself. So the editor understands Maximus thus: the manifestation and revelation of the thing believed and of God (which happens through the gifts of the Spirit that aid faith) is our comprehension and perception of it, so that we have him dwelling in us, present and most intimate, as in Paul (Eph. 3:17): 'that Christ dwell by faith in your hearts.' Nor does this forbid calling it a secret union and as it were a mingling, as Hesychius explains perichorei as 'is mingled'. But in these matters we stammer, although the Greeks are a little more fortunate in words. In other places Picus is hardly any more fortunate, as when he renders the 'ever-moving station' (aeikinetos stasis) as 'a condition always moving', not 'moved by perpetual impulse'; such as is that of those who enjoy God.

text: Τὴν μὲν σχετικήν. Nulla hic commodius voce reddi videatur, quam si intentionalem dicamus; quasi in animi rationibus et apprehensione positam; quam et abstractivam rudiori vocabulo nostri theologi vocant. Affinis usus illius vocis Patribus vii synodi, dum adorationem imaginum, quam sanciunt, σχετικὴν vocant; quæ scilicet non ad ipsam rem, ut in se est, terminatur, sed ut in sui similitudine, animo cogitanti quasi præsens objicitur, ac quadam in eam intentione ac motu, secundum quam dicitur honor imaginis transire ad exemp'ar seu prototypum. Nihil ad rem, quod Picus semel et iterum reconditam. Ac certe longe inauditum mundo, quod quis ex ejus interpretamentis conficeret vocabularium: sic sine judicio cuncta viro arbitraria; ut quod hic, ἡ μεθέξει κατ᾿ ἐνέργειαν γνῶσις, illi est cognitio est particeps operationis: quod ἔφεσιν, pro αἴσθησιν decoquit, etc.
anchorLine: τὴν μέν, σχετικὴν (o), ὡς ἐν λόγῳ μόνῳ κειμένην
en: 'The relational (knowledge).' The editor says no word renders it better than 'intentional', as if placed in the soul's reasonings and apprehension, which our theologians in cruder terminology also call 'abstractive'. The Fathers of the seventh council use the word similarly when they call the adoration of images that they approve 'relational', since it does not end in the thing itself as it is in itself but, as in its likeness, is presented to the thinking mind as present, with a certain intention and movement toward it, according to which the honour of the image is said to pass to the exemplar or prototype. The editor adds that Picus's repeated rendering 'reconditam' (hidden) is beside the point, and that it would be unheard of to compile a vocabulary from his interpretations, since all would be arbitrary and without judgment; as here, where 'knowledge by participation according to energy' is rendered by him 'knowledge is partaker of operation', and where he boils down 'ephesin' (desire) into 'aisthesin' (sense), etc.

anchorLine: τὴν αἴσθησιν [male edita, ἔφεσιν, cupiditatem], ἀφαι-
en: Bracketed Latin gloss: the editor says αἴσθησιν was wrongly edited (earlier printings), and gives ἔφεσιν ('desire', Latin cupiditatem) as the right reading. It is a correction/conjecture of the word, not a supply or deletion.

text: Ἀναιτίως προηγήσατο τῆς γενέσεως. Quod semel et iterum cavet Maximus, hoc et 39 cap. ne τὸ ἀναιτίως et ἀναίτιον, quasi innoxium et sine culpa accipiatur, quæ est proclivis ejus vocis acceptio, id vero propense Picus amplectitur, ac ubique interpretatur. Est certe hæc voluptas eo sensu haud ἀναίτιος, sed culpæ conjuncta, et ex culpa, ni magis ipsa culpa; ipse naturæ reatus ex transgressione, sic quasi brutæ vitæ, quæ libidine ducatur, nec jam ratione, sed magis sensu vivat: ἀναίτιος vero, id est sine causa, quod laborem, cui succedat, ejusque causa sit, nullum habeat. Unde nec Christus sic ἀναίτιον nativitatem ex libidine assumpsit, quod non illo modo ἀναίτιος, sed illi comitem laborem, exque illa, ὡς αἰτίας, ut eo juste, cum in illo injustus esset, nullo scilicet in ipso reatu, illam aboleret. Quam belle cohæret, ut Maximo ἀδικωτάτη, injustissima, sit hæc voluptas seu libido, et tamen ipsa ἀναίτιος sit, ipsa sine culpa, bello interprete Pico? Nec enim ut labor injustus, sic et voluptas; quod hæc a voluntate exsistat, ille ab exteriore agente.
anchorLine: προκαθηγήσατο τῆς γενέσεως (p). Ἀναίτιον δέ φημι
en: 'Without cause he went before the birth.' The editor says Maximus is twice careful (here and in chapter 39) that the words anaitios and anaition not be taken as 'innocent and without guilt', which is the easy sense of the word, though Picus eagerly embraces it and renders it so everywhere. This pleasure is certainly not anaitios in that sense, but joined to guilt and arising from guilt, if not itself guilt; he is himself liable by the transgression, as if of a brute life led by lust and no longer by reason but rather living by sense; 'anaitios', that is without cause, in that it has no labour which it follows or of which it is the cause. Hence Christ did not take birth from lust in the sense 'anaition' (as blameless) but as a labour accompanying it, and from it, as cause, so that he might justly abolish it, being himself unjust in nothing, with no guilt in himself. The editor asks how well it fits that for Maximus this pleasure, or lust, is 'most unjust' (adikotate) and yet is itself 'anaitios' (blameless), according to the elegant Picus; for pleasure is not unjust as toil is, since it arises from the will, while toil arises from an external agent.

text: Ex ead. quæst. 58 ex qua superiora αὐτολεξεί.
anchorLine: α'. * Ἐπινοητικὴν οἶδε τὴν νοερὰν τῆς ψυχῆς δύ-
en: From the same question, 58, from which the preceding passages are taken word for word.

text: Ἐπινοητικὴν οἶδε τὴν νοερὰν τῆς ψυχῆς δύναμιν. Expositio est ejus quod dixerat superiori, c. 100 τὴν τῶν ἡδέων ἐπινοητικὴν σχέσιν· sic passim, aliam alia sententia Maximus exponit, ac si esset diversus auctor. Esseque non raro suadeat Photii ipsa censura, a limine Quæst. ad Thalassium posita, et quod ipse quandoque deprehendi, Marci quædam αὐτολεξεί inserta aliis Maximi Capita. Refert ergo illud, οἶδε, superiorem auctorem, qui sic intellectum aut rationem, facultatem animi ἐπινοητικὴν (id est, excogitandi seu inveniendi solertem) quasi paraphrasi vocaverit, non divinam Scripturam aut sermonem, ut non bene reddidit Picus. Socus cum additur λόγος, uti quandoque facit Maximus, ac passim alii theologi.
anchorLine: ναμιν (l)· ἥτις χωριζομένη τῆς κατ᾿ αἴσθησιν σχέ-
en: 'He knows the inventive intellectual power of the soul.' The editor says this is an exposition of what the earlier passage (chapter 100, 'the inventive relation of pleasures') had said; Maximus often explains one idea by another, as if the author were a different person. Photius's own censure, set at the head of the Questions to Thalassius, urges this too, and the editor has himself noticed that Maximus sometimes inserts passages of Mark word for word among his other chapters. So the word 'oide' ('he knows') refers to the earlier author, who in a kind of paraphrase has called the intellect or reason, a faculty of the soul, 'epinoetic' (that is, clever at excogitating or inventing), not the divine Scripture or discourse, as Picus wrongly rendered it. [The printed 'Socus' is as it stands]: when 'logos' is added, as Maximus sometimes does and as other theologians commonly do.

text: [qq. ad Thalass., q. 58, ὧν κατ᾿ οὐσίαν ἀντιλαμ.]
en: Bracketed editorial reading from the Questions to Thalassius, q. 58: there the words run 'ὧν κατ᾿ οὐσίαν ἀντιλαμ[βάνεσθαι]' ('of which to apprehend according to essence'). A variant/parallel reading, not a supply or deletion.
